newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey affirms military backing for Turk Cypriots.
newsitem.headline: Turkey affirms military backing for Turk Cypriots.

text.p: Turkey pledged on Monday further military backing for Turkish Cypriots on the divided island of Cyprus in a row over the purchase of anti-aircraft missiles.

"Any aggression...directed against Turkey or the (Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus) TRNC will be jointly confronted and the military planning and coordination necessary for this will be done," the two sides said in a joint statement.
Tension on Cyprus has risen since the Cypriot government, in the Greek Cypriot-populated south, announced the planned purchase of S-300 missiles from Russia earlier this month.
"Those who attack the Turkish Cypriots are attacking Turkey. They should think about that," Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash told reporters after talks with Turkish President Suleyman Demirel.
The joint statement said Turkey and the Turkish Cypriots would establish "a joint military concept" on the island.
Turkey would build air force and naval bases on Cyprus if Greece continued "entrenching" itself on Cyprus. "Reciprocal military and political measures will be taken," it said.
Turkey, which sponsors the Turkish Cypriot enclave in the north of the island, has threatened to strike Greek Cypriot targets if the missile deployment goes ahead.
The missile row has again highlighted the volatility of one of the most heavily militarised areas in the world.

Turkey has 30,000 troops stationed on the island, which has been divided since 1974, when Turkey invaded the northern third in response to a coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece.
The internationally recognised Greek Cypriot government forces number a third of that.

Greece, worried already about its own weakness against Turkey's 639,000-strong forces -- Athens has 168,000 -- signed a military cooperation pact with Cyprus in 1993 and the two countries have worked to coordinate military strategy, exercises and equipment.
Turkey accuses Greece of steadily and provocatively arming Cyprus under the pact.

The Cyprus government has bought Exocet anti-ship missiles and more than 100 battle tanks from France in the past few years, it has bought armoured vehicles from Moscow and is still taking delivery of 40 Russian battle tanks.
Both Turkey and Greece are NATO members and have boosted their military arsenals and developed their defence industries through the alliance in recent years.
The Greek Cypriot administration says their latest acquisitions, the missiles, are purely defensive in view of their inferior military might, but Ankara sees them as a threat to Turkey itself.
The missiles' range of 90 miles (150 km) would allow them to knock out planes inside Turkish air space as well as compromise Turkey's air superiority over Cyprus.

U.S. envoy Carey Cavanaugh visited Athens, Nicosia and Ankara last week to try to dampen the missile row. After his trip he said a potential crisis had been averted because Cyprus vowed the S-300s would not be installed for 16 months.
Turkey has discounted Cavanaugh's optimism, saying the 16 months is meaningless because the missiles were not due to be delivered from Russia until mid-1998 anyway.
